article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: TCLAS High-Quality, Sustainable Residency Program grant
description: Launched in 2021 as part of the $1.4 billion Texas COVID Learning Acceleration Supports initiative underwritten by federal COVID-19 relief funds, the program "provided grant funding for paid placements supporting more than 2,100 residents at 85 school districts, offered in partnership with state-approved EPPs." Districts were required to partner with state-designated Vetted Teacher Residency programs. The grant also provided technical assistance for districts to adopt strategic staffing models intended to sustain paid residencies after grant funding ended in 2024.
requirements: Districts must partner with a state-designated Vetted Teacher Residency program to apply for funding
constraints: Grant funding ended in 2024, and some districts have struggled to maintain residency funding after grants ended
examples: Grant-funded districts focused on strengthening partnerships, collaborative planning and governance, and adopting strategic staffing changes in K–12 schools
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: The effects of generative AI on collaborative problem-solving and team creativity performance in digital story creation: an experimental study
citation: Wei, X., Wang, L., Lee, L.-K., & Liu, R. (2025). The effects of generative AI on collaborative problem-solving and team creativity performance in digital story creation: an experimental study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 22:23. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00526-0
title: Four-dimension team creative performance framework for DST evaluation (novelty, relevance, user experience, sustainability)
description: The study adopted Liu et al.'s (2023) TCP assessment framework comprising four dimensions: "novelty, relevance, user experience, and sustainability." Novelty assesses originality and innovation; relevance focuses on practical applicability; user experience evaluates engagement through authenticity, cultural immersion, and audience connection; sustainability considers long-term viability across environmental, cultural, and economic factors. The framework was operationalized with two to three criteria per dimension on a ten-point scale, weighted 30% each for sustainability and user experience and 20% each for novelty and relevance.
requirements: Evaluation requires multiple expert raters with high inter-rater consistency (ICC > 0.8)
constraints: Designed specifically for evaluating TCP in complex, collaborative DST contexts
target_learning_goals: team creativity performance in collaborative digital story creation
examples: Three experts (two in educational technology, one in DST research) rated six DST products per group using this framework, achieving ICC = 0.89
key_sources: Wei, X., Wang, L., Lee, L.-K., & Liu, R. (2025). The effects of generative AI on collaborative problem-solving and team creativity performance in digital story creation: an experimental study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 22:23. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00526-0

article_title: The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005
title: Fundamental-versus-peripheral hypothesis taxonomy specifies criteria for rejecting or failing to replicate the model
description: To answer criticisms that social-cognitive models are unfalsifiable, the authors classify each of the model's 23 hypotheses as fundamental or peripheral. Fundamental hypotheses test the three core propositions (H1-H5 and H15); peripheral hypotheses cover the belief-mediated pathways. The authors state that "Support for Hypotheses 1 to 5 is fundamental for the test of model to be accepted and a null finding for any of these hypotheses in an overall test of the model will render it rejected as a failed replication." Failure of peripheral hypotheses does not invalidate the core pathways, since mediation through any one belief-based construct suffices.
requirements: Any test must provide unequivocal support for the three model propositions and acceptance of all fundamental hypotheses
constraints: Component paths of indirect effects (e.g., H6-H8, H12-H14) need not all be supported for the indirect effects to be valid
target_learners: researchers testing motivational models in educational settings
target_learning_goals: evaluation of replication and falsification criteria for motivational theories
examples: Table 1 outlines the status of each hypothesis as fundamental or peripheral to supporting or rejecting the model
key_sources: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005

article_title: Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience
citation: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16
title: Pascual-Leone's Theory of Constructive Operators (TCO): mental-attentional capacity as measurable maturational driver of developmental stages
description: TCO is a neo-Piagetian causal model of organismic processing that explains Piaget's descriptive stage theory from a metasubjective perspective "from within the subject's own processes". Behaviour is generated by general-purpose hidden operators modulating self-propelling schemes under "a principle of overdetermination" whereby performance is determined by the dominant set of activated compatible schemes. It offers a theory-guided measurement method quantifying mental-attention demand of tasks and capacity per stage, with capacity increasing one symbolic-processing unit every other year after age 3, reaching seven units at about 15–16 years.
requirements: Process-task analysis to quantify the mental-attention demand of tasks and the mental-attentional capacity available at each developmental stage
constraints: Capacity of seven units is obtained only when all necessary schemes, figurative and operative, and their essential parameters have been counted; adults often function mobilising at most a capacity of five unless highly motivated and challenged
target_learners: children and adolescents across developmental stages
target_learning_goals: explaining cognitive-development constraints on task performance and problem solving
examples: The article applies TCO to advise against averaging brain responses across wide age ranges and to guide age-group selection via the trade-off between task mental demand and mental-attentional capacity
key_sources: Arsalidou, M. & Pascual-Leone, J. (2016). Constructivist developmental theory is needed in developmental neuroscience. npj Science of Learning 1, 16016. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.16

article_title: Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training
citation: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1
title: TC3Sim combat medic training simulation integrated with GIFT
description: TC3Sim (also known as vMedic) is a serious game used to train US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers on tactical combat casualty care tasks, including care under fire. It presents linearly structured scenarios with fixed event sequences while allowing learners to freely navigate 3D environments and choose how to administer casualty care. TC3Sim is integrated with the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT), which managed sensors, delivered pre-tests, training materials, post-tests, and run-time motivational feedback triggered by affect detectors. A downloadable version has been made publicly available.
requirements: GIFT integration for sensor management, assessment administration, and feedback delivery
constraints: Training scenarios are structured linearly, presenting a fixed series of events regardless of the learner's actions
target_learners: US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers
target_learning_goals: Tactical combat casualty care: hemorrhage control, care under fire, tactical field care, casualty evacuation
examples: Scenarios included a leg amputation/tourniquet task, a village scenario with enemy fire, and the Kobayashi Maru scenario where the soldier expires regardless of actions
key_sources: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1

article_title: Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training
citation: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1
title: Interaction-based frustration detector model for TC3Sim
description: A logistic regression detector of frustration induced from 39 features of learner interaction with TC3Sim, synchronized to BROMP field observations and validated with 10-fold participant-level cross-validation (Kappa = 0.105, A' = 0.692). Detection of player frustration was a function of enemy action affecting the player, patient status such as dangerously high heart rate and worsening condition, and the player's diagnostic actions, which were associated with less frustration. The detector was integrated into GIFT to trigger motivational feedback messages in later experiments.
requirements: Synchronization of trainee actions with BROMP field observations via the HART application
Feature engineering specific to the TC3Sim user interface and scenario events
constraints: Much of the creation of interaction-based detectors is specific to the system for which the detectors are created and must be replicated for new learning environments
target_learners: US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers in TC3Sim training
target_learning_goals: Detecting trainee frustration during tactical combat casualty care training to trigger supportive feedback
examples: The detector's weights included Sum of Systolic Change (1.08), Max of Heart Rate (1.04), and Total Number of Blood Sweep Actions (−0.07) over a 20 s time window
key_sources: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1

article_title: Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy
citation: Ale, K., Loh, Y. A.-C., & Chib, A. (2017). Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy. Education Tech Research Dev, 65, 769–794. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9517-2
title: Technology-Community-Management (TCM) model as a framework for contextualized technology implementation
description: The Technology-Community-Management model is the article's organizing framework for designing technology implementation around contextual factors. The article states that the "Contextualized-OLPC education project utilized strategies identified by the Technology-Community-Management model to address contextually germane factors of teacher training, unbiased gender access, and local language use." It is presented as a way to prioritize local contexts during technology implementation design.
requirements: Implementation design must address teacher training, unbiased gender access, and local language use as contextually germane factors.
target_learners: primary school students in rural developing-country contexts
key_sources: Ale, K., Loh, Y. A.-C., & Chib, A. (2017). Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy. Education Tech Research Dev, 65, 769–794. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9517-2

article_title: Game-based learning for ethics: benefits, challenges, and dilemmas
citation: Zvereva, G., Guillén, G., Al-Msallam, S., Hamari, J., & Xi, N. (2026). Game-based learning for ethics: benefits, challenges, and dilemmas. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10678-z
title: Social Cognitive Theory's Triadic Causation Model as a framework for mapping pedagogical dilemmas in ethics game design
description: Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory holds that "human behaviors result from the bidirectional dynamic interplay between environmental (social norms, external surroundings), behavioral (actions, practice, response, self-efficacy), and personal factors (knowledge, expectations, attitudes)". The study used this Triadic Causation Model as the analytical framework to depict the pedagogical dilemmas that developers of board games for ethics education should be aware of, categorizing each dilemma by its prevailing TCM dimension.
requirements: Dilemmas were formulated from underlying tensions first identified and mapped from benefit and challenge themes, with consensus among three researchers
constraints: The study aims to illuminate rather than resolve the dilemmas, and recognizes that additional factors beyond the two central tensions per TCM domain also play a role
examples: Each of the six identified dilemmas was categorized according to the behavioral, personal, or environmental TCM dimension in Table 2
key_sources: Zvereva, G., Guillén, G., Al-Msallam, S., Hamari, J., & Xi, N. (2026). Game-based learning for ethics: benefits, challenges, and dilemmas. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10678-z

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of Tactile-Cued Self-Monitoring Interventions Used by Students in Educational Settings
citation: McDougall, D., Ornelles, C., Mersberg, K., & Amona, K. (2015). A Meta-Analytic Review of Tactile-Cued Self-Monitoring Interventions Used by Students in Educational Settings. JAASEP. https://jaasep.org
title: Four-component model of behavioral self-management, with self-monitoring as its first two components
description: The review situates TCSM within the behavioral self-management (BSM) framework Glynn, Thomas, and Shee proposed in 1973, grounding it in the cognitive-behavioral modification principle of reactivity: when people become cognitively aware of their behavior and the environment, they are better positioned to change their behavior. As printed, "The first two components of their model, self-assessment plus self-recording, constitute self-monitoring." The remaining components are self-determination of reinforcement and self-administration of reinforcement, and the review notes BSM has since evolved to add techniques such as self-evaluation, video self-modeling, and self-graphing. The review uses this framework to organize its background and to define where tactile cues enter the self-assessment step.
requirements: Participants must use a tactile cue that prompts periodic self-assessment and self-recording of then-current behavior, not merely an initial behavior prompt
constraints: The review applies the model to students in educational settings, mostly students with disabilities aged 10 to 15
target_learners: students with disabilities in elementary, middle, and high school educational settings
target_learning_goals: self-directed behavior change and academic engagement through self-assessment and self-recording
examples: The nine qualifying studies operationalized self-assessment questions such as "Am I working quickly?" with tactile cues from a MotivAider or vibrating wristwatch, followed by self-recording on paper forms
key_sources: McDougall, D., Ornelles, C., Mersberg, K., & Amona, K. (2015). A Meta-Analytic Review of Tactile-Cued Self-Monitoring Interventions Used by Students in Educational Settings. JAASEP. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1134294

article_title: Effect of Jigsaw I Technique on Teaching Turkish Grammar
citation: Akif ARSLAN. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw I technique on teaching Turkish grammar. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2709
title: Turkish Course Attitude Scale (TCAS)
description: A 20-item five-point Likert attitude scale from the Middle School Turkish Course Teaching Program and Guide (2006), with eight reverse-coded adverse items. Reliability was tested with Cronbach Alpha on data from 200 students outside the study scope, yielding "a high value of α = 0,856" indicating high reliability. Item-deletion analyses showed four items contributed only partially to internal consistency, but the instrument structure was retained given the sampling-size caveat.
requirements: Cronbach Alpha of 0.70 or more for overall and each factor, per the cited Hair et al. criterion
constraints: Four items showed only partial contribution to internal consistency, which the author attributes to possible sampling-size effects
examples: Administered as pretest and posttest to both experimental and control groups
key_sources: Akif ARSLAN. (2016). Effect of Jigsaw I technique on teaching Turkish grammar. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2709

article_title: Measuring Teacher Implementation of the "BEST in CLASS" Intervention Program and Corollary Child Outcomes
citation: Conroy, M. A., Sutherland, K. S., Algina, J. J., Wilson, R. E., Martinez, J. R., & Whalon, K. J. (2014). Measuring Teacher Implementation of the BEST in CLASS Intervention Program and Corollary Child Outcomes. Journal of Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/1063426614532949
title: TCIDOS-RV2.1 behavioral observation coding system
description: The Teacher–Child Interaction Direct Observation System–Research Version 2.1 is a researcher-developed partial-interval coding system designed to record and code teachers' use of BEST in CLASS instructional practices and related teacher and child responses. Observers code 15-min sessions of sixty 15-s intervals using the Lily software; inter-observer reliability estimates per code averaged between 89% and 99%.
requirements: Observer training to a criterion of at least 80% agreement on each code across master-coded videotapes
constraints: It only provides an estimate of the occurrence of each code and has not been validated; it does not include a measure of the quality of the responses
target_learners: Early childhood teachers and their focal children
target_learning_goals: Measuring implementation fidelity of instructional practices and child behavior outcomes
examples: Used at baseline, post-test, and maintenance time points during naturally occurring teacher-directed instructional time
key_sources: Conroy, M. A., Sutherland, K. S., Algina, J. J., Wilson, R. E., Martinez, J. R., & Whalon, K. J. (2014). Measuring Teacher Implementation of the BEST in CLASS Intervention Program and Corollary Child Outcomes. Journal of Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/1063426614532949

article_title: Team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning in medical postgraduates training.
citation: Huang Tianlong, Zhou Shun, Wei Qiaoyan, Ding Chun. (2024). Team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning in medical postgraduates training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05650-5
title: TCLEBL: an integrated team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning model for medical postgraduate education
description: TCLEBL combines four pedagogies the article describes separately: team-based learning's collaborative group work, case-based learning's authentic clinical vignettes, retained lecture components for structured knowledge frameworks, and evidence-based learning built on literature retrieval and critical appraisal. In the studied implementation, students worked in two teams on an ocular toxocariasis case, performed pre-class literature searches for "the latest scientific research, clinical trials, meta-analyses, and systematic evaluations", presented diagnostic and treatment plans in class with teacher guidance, and wrote a review article afterwards. The model aims to "provide a comprehensive, well-rounded teaching experience in medical postgraduate education".
requirements: A teacher who instructs both content delivery and evidence-synthesis guidance; pre-selected case records; access to academic databases, medical journals, and specialty guidelines; assessment via theory exams and written literature reviews.
constraints: Evaluated only in ophthalmology postgraduates at a single institution, on a single disease topic not covered in standard five-year ophthalmology textbooks.
target_learning_goals: literature searching, critical appraisal, and review writing
examples: 41 ophthalmology postgraduates were divided into a TCLEBL group (n = 21) and an LBL group (n = 20), with the same teacher and consistent teaching content in both groups.
key_sources: Huang Tianlong, Zhou Shun, Wei Qiaoyan, Ding Chun. (2024). Team-, case-, lecture- and evidence-based learning in medical postgraduates training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05650-5
